planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in deep, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; China fir tolerates summer heat and humidity better than most true firs, making it a substitute conifer for warm-temperate gardens where Abies species struggle.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring, spacing them well back from structures in deep, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and water regularly through the first two seasons while roots establish. China fir forms a broad pyramidal tree with stiff, glossy, dark green needles borne in dense whorled tiers, and old bark exfoliates in long reddish-brown strips that add winter interest. Unlike many needled conifers it resprouts vigorously from cut stumps and tolerates the humid summers of the southeastern United States, where it is grown as a large screening or specimen tree rather than the timber crop it forms across much of China. Lower branches often decline with age and can be limbed up to reveal the trunk on mature specimens.
sources: USDA Forest Service Woody Plant Seed Manual

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown trees in spring or fall in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Douglas fir needs cool nights and consistent moisture and struggles in hot, humid, or poorly drained sites.

directions: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown trees in spring or fall in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, allowing generous room to grow since this is one of the largest conifers in North America. Douglas fir carries soft, flat, blue-green to dark green needles and distinctive pendulous cones with three-pointed bracts that protrude past each scale, a reliable identification feature unique among conifers. It is among the most important timber trees on the continent and is also the most widely grown Christmas tree species in cooler climates, valued in the landscape for dense pyramidal form and a strong central leader. Performance declines sharply outside cool, humid, well-drained mountain and coastal climates, so it is a poor choice for the hot, humid Southeast or dry, alkaline plains soils.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; Norfolk Island pine tolerates salt spray and wind, which is why it is so often planted along subtropical and tropical coastlines.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to partial shade, and protect young trees from frost, since foliage is damaged well above freezing. Despite the common name this is not a true pine but a member of the ancient Araucariaceae family, forming a strikingly symmetrical, tiered, pagoda-like silhouette with horizontal branches of soft, needle-like foliage that make it a favorite avenue and specimen tree along Florida, Gulf Coast, and southern California coastlines. It tolerates salt spray and sandy soils better than most conifers, but outside frost-free zones it is more commonly kept as a container specimen or houseplant, where it stays much smaller than the 100-foot trees seen in its native range and along tropical streets.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil of average fertility in full sun to partial shade; African fern pine tolerates heat, drought once established, and urban conditions, and is commonly clipped as a hedge or espalier as well as grown as a specimen tree.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil of average fertility in full sun to partial shade, watering regularly the first year and then only occasionally once roots are established, since this East African conifer handles heat and drought far better than most needled evergreens. Fine, narrow, willowy leaves give the tree a soft, weeping texture unlike the stiff scale foliage of junipers and cypresses commonly used for the same purposes, and it responds well to shearing, which makes it a popular clipped hedge, screen, or espalier as well as an unclipped specimen tree in mild climates. It is widely planted as a street and parking-lot tree in California and the Southwest for its tolerance of reflected heat, compacted soil, and irregular irrigation, but is damaged by hard freezes and is only reliable outdoors in nearly frost-free zones.
sources: UC Davis Arboretum and Public Garden

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Yoshino' holds its rich green color through winter better than the straight species, which often bronzes in cold weather.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and mulch to keep roots cool and evenly moist through summer heat. 'Yoshino' is one of the most widely planted Japanese cedar selections in American gardens because its dense, soft, blue-green foliage stays green through winter rather than turning the bronze-purple typical of the species, and its broadly pyramidal form and faster growth rate suit it well to screening and hedging. It reaches a moderate mature size compared with the towering wild species, making it a more practical choice for residential-scale privacy plantings while still providing the fine, feathery texture Japanese cedar is prized for.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Black Dragon' keeps its very dark green color year-round and stays far more compact than the species.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, siting them where their dense form can be appreciated up close along a path or foundation bed. 'Black Dragon' is a slow-growing, densely branched dwarf selection of Japanese cedar with tightly packed, curled, near-black-green foliage that holds its color through winter without the bronzing common in larger cultivars. Its compact, irregularly conical to globose habit fits rock gardens, mixed conifer collections, and small-space foundation plantings where a full-sized Japanese cedar would quickly overwhelm the space.

common_name: Globosa Nana Japanese Cedar (Dwarf Globe Sugi)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Globosa Nana' forms a naturally rounded mound and needs little to no pruning to keep its shape.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants to allow their naturally rounded outline to develop without crowding. 'Globosa Nana' is one of the oldest and most popular dwarf Japanese cedar selections, forming a dense, symmetrical mound of soft, blue-green, slightly twisted needles that take on a plum-bronze cast in cold weather before greening up again in spring. Its predictable globe shape and slow growth make it a dependable anchor plant in mixed conifer gardens, foundation plantings, and Asian-style landscapes where a formal, low-maintenance mass is wanted without shearing.

common_name: Otto Luyken Cherry Laurel (Dwarf English Laurel)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Otto Luyken' stays low and dense without shearing, making it a standard low hedge and foundation shrub in shaded sites.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun, and water regularly the first year to establish a dense root system before drier summers. 'Otto Luyken' is a compact, low-mounding selection of cherry laurel with narrower, glossier leaves than the species and abundant upright spikes of small white flowers in mid-spring, followed by small black fruits that birds favor. Its naturally tidy, spreading habit and shade tolerance make it one of the most reliable low hedges and mass foundation plantings for shaded entryways and woodland-edge borders, requiring only occasional shaping rather than regular shearing to stay dense.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Schip laurel is noticeably more cold hardy than most cherry laurel selections, tolerating colder winters without foliage burn.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun, allowing enough room for its arching, spreading branches to fill in as an informal hedge. Schip laurel carries narrower, smaller, more finely textured leaves than the species along with the same fragrant white spring flower spikes and dark fruit, but it was selected in the Balkan mountains for improved cold hardiness, so it holds up in colder winters that damage many other cherry laurel cultivars. Its dense, layered growth and tolerance of shade and shearing have made it a widely used privacy hedge and screening plant in the Pacific Northwest and mid-Atlantic where a fast, reliably evergreen barrier is needed.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; 'Jeddeloh' develops a distinctive nest-like depression at the center of the plant as it ages and needs consistent moisture, never drying out completely.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in a site sheltered from full afternoon sun and drying winds, and keep the root zone consistently moist since hemlocks do not tolerate drought. 'Jeddeloh' is a dwarf, mounding selection of eastern hemlock with fine, soft, dark green needles on branches that radiate outward and slightly downward, forming the shallow central depression that gives nest-form conifers their name. Its slow growth and low, spreading shape suit it to rock gardens, shaded foundation plantings, and mixed dwarf conifer collections rather than screening, and, like all eastern hemlocks, it should be monitored for hemlock woolly adelgid in regions where that pest is established.
